title: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
desc: Finds persistent task-dependent errors despite retrieval, fine-tuning and checking, making review a disputed productivity cost.

kps.k: Legal GenAI can assist research, drafting and analysis, but fluent output is not self-authenticating legal work.
kps.d: The cluster’s central proposition is that probabilistic text generation can produce useful work while fabricating authorities, misquoting genuine sources, misstating holdings or relying on inapplicable law. The harder risk is often not an obviously nonexistent case but a plausible proposition attached to a real authority that does not support it. Confidence, detail and authoritative tone can conceal both kinds of error, so apparent sophistication does not establish legal accuracy or sound reasoning.

kps.k: Empirical evidence establishes material reliability problems, but no single error rate represents legal AI generally.
kps.d: Large Legal Fictions found high factual-error rates when public, general-purpose models answered structured questions about federal cases. The Stanford RegLab study of proprietary legal research tools found lower—but still substantial—hallucination rates despite retrieval-augmented generation. A later longitudinal citation study found that obvious fabricated-citation rates did not decline consistently across successive ChatGPT models. These results concern different models, dates, tasks and definitions: legal knowledge recall, difficult research queries and citation fabrication are not interchangeable measures.

qs.q: In total, we execute more than 800,000 queries—200,000+ per LLM—and we share our raw API calls and model responses in the replication materials accompanying this article.
qs.a: Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models · Academia · 2024

qs.q: to general-purpose chatbots (GPT-4), we find that the AI research tools made by                                                     LexisNexis (Lexis+ AI) and Thomson Reuters (Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and                                                     Ask Practical Law AI) each hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Retrieval, fine-tuning, reasoning models and automated checking mitigate risk without establishing error-free performance.
kps.d: Grounding models in legal databases can reduce fabrication, expose underlying sources and improve task performance. Randomised evidence also indicates that RAG and reasoning-model assistance can improve the quality and productivity of human legal work on tested tasks. Disagreement centres on degree: some vendors and commentators expect database access and better models to make outright fabrication readily avoidable, while independent testing finds residual retrieval, applicability and reasoning failures. Automated checking likewise improves detection but still struggles with pincites, misquotations and substantive misrepresentation.

qs.q: We ﬁnd that both AI tools signiﬁcantly enhance legal work quality, a marked contrast with previous research examining older large language models like GPT-4.
qs.a: AI-Powered Lawyering: AI Reasoning Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and the Future of Legal Practice · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Agentic retrieval improves recall by 26.2% over       non-agentic baselines on GPT-5, but all models struggle most with incorrect pincites, verbatim       misquotes, and content misrepresentation (52.8%, 95.2%, and 83.2% recall for GPT-5 respec-       tively).
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

kps.k: The dominant professional response is verification before reliance, under duties that pre-date generative AI.
kps.d: Courts, bar bodies and professional guidance generally permit careful AI assistance rather than prohibit it. They place nondelegable responsibility on lawyers to check every material citation, quotation, fact and legal proposition against authoritative sources, including whether an authority remains good law and actually supports the asserted proposition. Existing competence, supervision, candour and filing-certification rules supply the principal framework. Court incidents document sanctions, costs orders, referrals and other consequences when lawyers or litigants submit fabricated or unsupported material; those incidents show realised harm but do not measure model error rates.

qs.q: To ethically use generative AI in the practice of law—which we do not dispute can be helpful if done properly and carefully—a lawyer must “ensure that the legal propositions and authority generated are trustworthy.” ByoPlanet Int’l, LLC v.

qs.a: Lnu v. Blanche, No. 24-4790 (9th Cir. June 3, 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Verification creates a disputed value problem rather than a settled answer about productivity.
kps.d: Optimistic accounts point to faster drafting, better retrieval and measured gains in AI-assisted student work. The counterargument is that lawyers must inspect every proposition because even rare errors can carry severe consequences, potentially consuming the time saved. Judges report avoiding AI research when verification produces no net saving, while the verification-value critique treats lower net utility as a hypothesis requiring empirical testing. The evidence therefore supports task-specific efficiency gains, not a general conclusion about net value in professional deployment; real-world evaluation must measure time to acceptable quality, checking costs and downstream effects.

qs.q: Several judges noted that this need for oversight is in tension with the benefit of GenAI as a time saver, and that they do not use GenAI for legal research because of this: they ultimately felt it did not save them time in the end.
qs.a: Judicial Use of Generative AI: Lessons Learned · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Assuming such a slowing of efficiency gains, it is posited that any increase in that variable will be met by a greater verification cost; verification will take on even more importance, given the emphasis on accuracy and truth imposed on lawyers by professional practice standards and the law (discussed below).
qs.a: The Verification-Value Paradox: A Normative Critique of Gen AI Use in Legal Practice · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Users’ legal capability and access to authoritative data determine who can benefit safely.
kps.d: Lawyers can often formulate better prompts, recognise suspect output and consult commercial databases; self-represented litigants and low-income users may lack each safeguard. The same people who could gain most from affordable explanations and drafting support may be least able to detect false premises, jurisdictional mistakes or misrepresented law, exposing them to sanctions, dismissal or worsened legal positions. Unmet legal need nevertheless makes continued consumer use likely. Practical responses include legal-data access, targeted AI literacy, supervised or bounded use cases and human-centred quality standards that assess legal and life outcomes rather than accuracy alone.

qs.q: 24  fragile and more akin to “pattern matching more than true logical reasoning.”132 Since nonlawyers often do not know which facts are legally salient, they will be unable to craft prompts that produce reliable outputs.
qs.a: Equal Justice and Generative AI · Academia · 2025

qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

kps.k: The debate extends beyond fabricated citations to quality, fairness, confidentiality and institutional trust.
kps.d: Citation verification does not establish that analysis is persuasive, complete, contextually appropriate or fair. Sources also raise opaque reasoning, prompt sensitivity, biased or unrepresentative data, confidentiality exposure and the possible weakening of professional judgment. Judicial use adds concerns about explainability, perceived fairness and public confidence. Accordingly, practical governance should combine use-case risk assessment, secure data practices, human review, task-specific audits and transparent benchmarking rather than reduce responsible use to checking whether cited cases exist.

qs.q: And yet, new evidence suggests that the risk of low-quality AI-supported legal work cannot be dismissed merely by requiring lawyers to check the veracity of AI-generated citations.
qs.a: Thinking Like a Lawyer in the Age of Generative AI: Cognitive Limits on AI Adoption Among Lawyers · Academia · 2025

qs.q: We believe that output verification will require both (a) additional auditing of AI systems, and (b) keeping humans in the loop.
qs.a: Tasks and Roles in Legal AI: Data Curation, Annotation, and Verification · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition’s core: legal GenAI can improve research, drafting and analysis, but retrieval, fine-tuning, reasoning models and automated checking do not make outputs self-authenticating or remove the need for verification. They materially develop that proposition through structured and preregistered evaluations of public and proprietary systems, randomized evidence of task-specific gains from human–AI assistance, longitudinal testing of fabricated citations, and benchmarks showing that agentic verification still misses subtle errors. They also broaden the analysis beyond model accuracy to verification costs, overconfidence and authoritative tone, uneven access to legal knowledge and databases, nonlawyers’ limited verification capacity, professional education, outcome-focused quality standards, confidentiality, fairness and institutional trust. Internal variation is material but does not overturn the overall direction: some work is optimistic about substantial productivity gains or future automated safeguards, while treating those gains as task-specific or prospective; the verification-value paradox argues that checking may erode net value but expressly presents that as a hypothesis requiring empirical testing. One scholarship-focused source redirects the debate from reliability to the loss of published work’s authorship-certification function, arguing that even flawless machine output would leave that institutional problem unresolved. Bibliographic-only excerpts provide no determinable position. These patterns describe the supplied selection, not academia or researchers generally.

qs.q: We find that legal RAG can reduce hallucinations compared to general-purpose AI systems (here, GPT-4), but hallucinations remain substantial, wide-ranging, and potentially insidious.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Our ﬁndings also show that these AI tools signiﬁcantly boost productivity in ﬁve out of six tested legal tasks, with statistically signiﬁcant gains of anywhere from 50% to 130%.
qs.a: AI-Powered Lawyering: AI Reasoning Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and the Future of Legal Practice · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The selected traditional-law-firm evidence accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that legal GenAI can produce useful drafts and research assistance but cannot make its own output reliable; competent human verification remains necessary. It materially develops that proposition through Allens’s Australian-law benchmarking, which identifies poor critical reasoning, fabricated or unauthoritative authorities, and the importation of UK and EU analysis without recognising jurisdictional differences. The sources also distinguish task-specific utility from dependable legal advice: routine drafting, summarisation and high-level research appear more promising than critical reasoning or jurisdiction-sensitive analysis. Internal variation is mainly one of emphasis rather than position. The earlier benchmark stresses concrete testing failures and careful review, while the 2025 account advances the broader argument that some limitations arise from probabilistic generation rather than merely inadequate training, while still expecting safeguards and models to improve. Both qualify their findings by model date, task and benchmark scope. Because these are curated Allens materials, this conclusion characterises the supplied law-firm voice and should not be generalised to traditional firms as a whole.

qs.q: However, inconsistencies in the performance of even the best-performing model means the draft still needs careful review by someone able to verify it is accurate and correct, and that it does not contain irrelevant or fictitious citations.
qs.a: Lawyer or language model? Testing AI's competence in answering Australian legal questions (The Allens AI Australian Law Benchmark) · Law firms · 2024

qs.q: The responses frequently adopted analysis from larger jurisdictions (especially the EU and the UK) without recognising the difference in the law.
qs.a: Lawyer or language model? Testing AI's competence in answering Australian legal questions (The Allens AI Australian Law Benchmark) · Law firms · 2024

vlens.an: This curated legal-tech-vendor voice supports the proposition overall: the sources generally accept that fluent legal-AI output can contain fabricated material, inaccurate legal interpretations or unfamiliar logical errors, and that lawyers must verify output against authoritative sources before relying on it. Common reasons include models’ incomplete grounding in legal data, the persistence of errors as reasoning improves, and professional duties requiring lawyers to check whether authorities are valid, relevant and accurately quoted. Several sources also argue that legal-specific databases, citation tools and other safeguards reduce risk, but mostly treat these measures as mitigation rather than substitutes for human review. Material internal variation concerns how durable the problem is. Pereyra recognises persistent logical mistakes while leaving open longer-term autonomous workflows; Fitzpatrick stresses both system improvement and lawyers’ pre-existing professional responsibilities; and the accountability source extends verification duties across lawyers, litigants and judges. Von Zastrow is the principal qualification: he characterises outright fabrication as readily avoidable in current legal-tech products and attributes many remaining errors to lack of case-law database access. That claim conflicts with the synthesis’s stronger conclusion that retrieval cannot eliminate residual applicability, quotation and reasoning failures, but it does not outweigh the broader acceptance within these selected sources that current output remains fallible. The sources offer mainly professional judgments, product explanations and predictions rather than comparative performance measurements, and this curated selection should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: As the models get better, the reasoning improves, but they still make logical mistakes.
qs.a: When Will Lawyers Trust AI? — Gabe Pereyra (Harvey) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources overall support the proposition that mitigation does not make legal GenAI output self-authenticating and that human verification remains necessary. Their common reasons are reported hallucination incidents, the difficulty of detecting plausible misrepresentations of genuine authorities, and concrete consequences when unchecked output reaches court filings. Material variation lies chiefly in evidentiary strength and emphasis: one podcast skeptically contrasts vendors’ “hallucination-free” promotion with continuing incidents but provides no vendor-specific testing; another questions the attention paid to hallucination cases without developing a position on residual error or verification; and the reported court cases give the clearest support through documented errors, sanctions and an express recommendation to check AI work. These sources do not establish a general model error rate or resolve whether verification eliminates net productivity gains, and this curated selection should not be treated as representative of the wider professional group.

vlens.an: This curated set of regulators, courts and professional bodies strongly supports the principal proposition. Across the sources, the common position is that generative AI may assist legal research, drafting, analysis and judicial administration, but fluent or authoritative-sounding output is not self-authenticating. Their recurring reasons are documented fabricated authorities and subtler misstatements of real cases; residual errors despite grounding, retrieval or legal specialisation; and lawyers’ pre-existing duties of competence, candour, supervision and accuracy. The resulting professional response is generally careful use rather than prohibition, with verification treated as a nondelegable human responsibility and failed checking linked to sanctions, costs, referrals and risks to institutional trust. Material variation concerns degree and emphasis. Some sources anticipate improving models, task-dependent risk and genuine efficiency gains; others are more sceptical that grounding or nominal human approval addresses deficient legal reasoning. Judicial experience and professional research also differ on productivity: some report that verification can erase time savings, while another source develops a real-world evaluation framework and treats net utility as an empirical question. Several guides broaden the analysis beyond accuracy to confidentiality, bias, fairness and transparency. One bibliographic-only LexRubric excerpt is insufficient to establish a position. These patterns describe the selected sources only and should not be treated as representative prevalence within the wider professional group.

qs.q: Attorneys cannot delegate that role to AI, computers, robots, or any other form of technology.

elens.an:
The curated 2023–2024 sources accept the proposition’s core claim and materially develop its evidentiary and governance foundations. They commonly reason that probabilistic generation can produce plausible but fabricated, misquoted or jurisdictionally inapplicable legal material, while confidence and fluency do not authenticate an answer. Court incidents and ethics guidance translate that concern into a professional rule: lawyers may use generative AI as assistance, but must independently verify citations, summaries and substantive propositions before reliance. Large Legal Fictions and the Allens Australian benchmark extend the proposition with structured testing showing task-dependent errors, overconfidence, false-premise acceptance, poor critical reasoning and jurisdiction-specific failures. Other sources broaden responsible evaluation beyond citation accuracy to real-world legal tasks, stakeholder-defined outcomes, bias and representativeness.

Material variation concerns degree and outlook rather than the central need for scrutiny. Some sources anticipate fewer hallucinations, automated checking and substantial drafting savings; Judge Newsom also treats risk as task-dependent. More critical accounts argue that predictive generation is not legal analysis or that nominal human approval is insufficient. A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law distinguishes fabricated citations from potentially defensible surrounding arguments. Several sources acknowledge that retrieval, better data or other mitigation may help, but the period evidence does not demonstrate that these measures eliminate residual error or human verification. Nor does it settle the proposition’s productivity-cost component: claimed time savings are principally prospective, while the supplied 2023–2024 evidence does not directly measure whether verification consumes those gains. This assessment characterises only the curated sources, not all commentary or institutions from the period.

qs.q: Performance degrades fur- ther on the most complex Core legal question and Central holding tasks, with hallucinations arising in response to at least 59% and 63% of our queries, respectively.
qs.a: Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.
qs.a: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 — Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources accept the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develop it. Their common reasoning is that legal GenAI can assist research, drafting, summarisation and analysis, but fluent output remains vulnerable to fabricated authorities, misquotation, mischaracterised holdings, inapplicable law and subtler misgrounding. Independent testing of proprietary legal-research tools strengthens the proposition by finding that retrieval-augmented generation reduces errors relative to general-purpose systems without eliminating them. Courts, professional guidance and practitioner-oriented sources consequently treat verification as a continuing, nondelegable responsibility grounded in pre-existing duties of competence, supervision and candour. Several sources extend the proposition further: they identify authoritative tone and verification drift as causes of misplaced reliance; show that nonlawyers may lack the legal knowledge or database access needed to verify outputs; recommend task-specific audits and deployment evaluation; and frame verification time as an unresolved empirical constraint on net productivity. Material internal variation concerns degree and remedy rather than the basic existence of risk. Some sources report strong task-specific performance, safeguards or RAG-enabled reductions in fabricated citations, and one founder argues that outright fabrication is now readily avoidable through database access. Others contend that errors are structural, difficult for humans or automated methods to detect, and extend beyond citations to reasoning quality, confidentiality, bias, fairness and institutional trust. A bibliography supplies no attributable position. These sources are a curated selection, so their alignment cannot be treated as evidence of prevalence across the legal sector.

qs.q: We find that legal RAG can reduce hallucinations compared to general-purpose AI systems (here, GPT-4), but hallucinations remain substantial, wide-ranging, and potentially insidious.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources accept the synthesis’s core proposition and materially develop it with several distinct forms of evidence. Courts and professional guidance permit careful GenAI assistance but treat verification as a nondelegable responsibility under existing competence, candour and filing rules; they increasingly emphasise that the danger includes plausible misstatements of genuine authorities, not only fabricated cases. Empirical work strengthens the mitigation claim: longitudinal testing finds that fabricated-citation rates do not consistently decline across model generations, while agentic retrieval improves detection but continues to miss subtle pincite, quotation and substantive-support errors. At the same time, randomized evidence shows that RAG and reasoning-model assistance can produce substantial quality and productivity gains on tested student tasks, so the period does not support a blanket claim that verification always eliminates value. Instead, interview evidence from judges, the Victorian report’s focus on time to acceptable quality, and the verification-value critique sharpen the unresolved question of net productivity after checking. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than broad rejection: some sources focus on sanctions and professional accountability; others on technical mitigation, legal-data access and AI literacy; Harvey’s Pereyra leaves open longer-term autonomy while accepting present errors and oversight; and one scholarship source redirects from reliability to the separate collapse of scholarship’s authorship-certification function. Bibliographic-only and truncated excerpts remain indeterminate. These sources are a curated selection and therefore establish neither the prevalence of these views nor consensus across the wider legal sector.

qs.q: Through a controlled experiment querying eight generations of ChatGPT models on 92 legal drafting prompts, we find that hallucination rates are no longer consistently decreasing across model generations, with GPT-5.1 producing hallucinated citations at a significantly higher rate than the best mid-2024 GPT-4o release (p = 0.001).
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026
